opus-5.5.text:
I think it's moving fast, but we should be honest about where the progress really is and where it isn't yet.

What's clearly worked is borrowing the recipe from vision and language: take a large pretrained model that already understands images and text, then attach an action head and fine-tune on robot data. These vision-language-action models give you much better semantic generalization. You can say "put the fruit in the blue bowl," and the robot handles objects or phrasings it never saw during robot training, because that knowledge comes from internet-scale pretraining. A few years ago that would have taken a lot of hand engineering.

But I'd separate semantics from physics. These models know *what* to do much better than they know *how* to do it. The hard part of robotics is contact, force, dexterity, recovering when something slips. That knowledge mostly isn't in internet text or static images. So you get a robot that understands the instruction beautifully and then fumbles the grasp. Language models are a strong prior for high-level planning, but the low-level, embodied understanding is still thin.

That's part of why I care so much about visual representation and world models. Language is a compressed, human-made abstraction of the world. It's useful, but much of what a robot needs, like spatial structure, dynamics, and how things deform or move, is better learned from vision and from interaction. I don't think we'll get there by putting a language model at the center and treating everything else as an adapter. We need models that understand the physical world more directly, that can predict what happens when you act, and then plan with that.

Data is the other bottleneck. Vision and language had the internet. Robotics has nothing comparable. People are trying teleoperation at scale, simulation, and learning from human videos. Video is especially interesting to me because there's so much of it and it implicitly contains physics and human manipulation. But turning passive video into actionable knowledge is still an open research problem.

So my overall assessment is real progress, especially in generalization and in the field converging on scalable recipes. But we're closer to robotics' "GPT-2 moment" than its "ChatGPT moment." The foundations are being laid, and I think the next breakthroughs will come less from bigger language backbones and more from better ways for models to see, understand space, and model the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Saining: I think it's one of the most exciting directions right now, but I'd also say we should be honest about where we actually are. If you look at what's happened in language and vision over the past few years, the recipe was pretty clear: scale the data, scale the model, and you get these emergent capabilities. People naturally want to transfer that recipe to robotics, and the intuition makes sense. A robot needs to perceive the world, understand instructions, reason about what to do, and then act. Vision-language models already handle the first two or three pieces reasonably well, so why not just bolt on the action part?

And to be fair, the progress has been real. Things like RT-2, OpenVLA, pi-zero, these vision-language-action models have shown that you can take a pretrained VLM, fine-tune it on robot trajectories, and get a policy that generalizes to new objects, new instructions, even some new scenes. A few years ago that would have been hard to imagine. The internet-scale semantic knowledge in those models is genuinely useful for robots. If I say "pick up the thing you'd use to cut paper," the model knows that means scissors, and that kind of common-sense grounding used to be very hard to get.

But here's where I'd push back a little. The fundamental bottleneck isn't really the model architecture. It's data, and it's the nature of the data. Language models learned from trillions of tokens of human text that already exist. Robots don't have that. Every demonstration has to be collected physically, with real hardware, in real time, and it's expensive and slow. Open X-Embodiment is a great effort, but it's still tiny compared to what we're used to in other modalities. So a lot of the "planning" these models do is really a kind of interpolation within a relatively small distribution of demonstrations.

The other thing I keep coming back to, and this connects to my own interests in representation learning, is that I don't think we've solved visual understanding at the level a robot actually needs. Current VLMs are quite good at semantics, at naming things, but they're surprisingly weak at spatial reasoning, at understanding geometry, physics, contact, how objects deform. We've seen in our own work that these models can fail on very basic visual questions that any child would get right. And for a robot, that's exactly the layer that matters. You can have perfect high-level planning, "open the drawer, take out the cup," but if the model doesn't really understand where the drawer handle is in 3D or how much force it takes, the plan is useless.

So my assessment is something like this: high-level task planning with language models, that's pretty mature and useful. Low-level control through VLA models, that's promising and improving fast, but still brittle and very data-hungry. And the middle layer, a genuine visual world model that understands space and physics well enough to support planning, I think that's the piece that's still missing. That's where I'd put my attention. Whether it comes from video generation models, from better self-supervised visual representations, from simulation, or some combination, I'm not sure yet. But I don't think you get robust robot planning until perception is actually solved, and we're not there.

astra-6.text:
I think the progress is exciting, but we need to distinguish between a model that can describe a sensible plan and a robot that can actually execute it. If you ask a model how to clean a table, it can break that task into steps. But picking up a glass requires understanding its position, making contact, controlling force, and adjusting when something unexpected happens. A good verbal plan doesn’t automatically solve those problems.

What’s promising is that models can provide a more general interface between instructions, perception, and action. Instead of building a separate system for every task, we can start thinking about systems that reuse knowledge across tasks. But reliability is still the key question. Can the robot succeed in a different room, with unfamiliar objects, and recover when its first attempt fails?

So I’m optimistic, but I would judge progress by that ability to adapt and recover, rather than by how impressive a single demonstration looks. The important step is closing the loop: act, observe what changed, and revise the plan.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the progress is exciting, but we should distinguish between a model that can describe a plan and a robot that can reliably execute it. A model might say, “Pick up the cup and put it on the table,” but that leaves a lot unresolved: how to grasp it, how much force to apply, and what to do if it slips or something blocks the path.

The opportunity is to connect the broad understanding of these models with perception, action, and feedback. The robot needs to observe what actually happened and adjust, rather than simply follow a sequence of instructions.

I also think data is a major bottleneck. Learning from text or images is very different from learning through physical interaction. So I’m optimistic about using advances in AI models for planning, but I would judge progress by how well a system handles unfamiliar situations and recovers from mistakes. That’s a much stronger test than completing a carefully prepared demonstration.
